chapter: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
title: Musicians as writers: Rex Stewart and Louis Armstrong
summary: They discuss Rex Stewart's writing and the editing it required. Hodes also praises Louis Armstrong's small booklet about early funerals.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Rex Stewart comes to mind right away.

Rex was a good writer, all he had to do was take the first two pages of his manuscript and throw those away, and then after he got through with all the pretensions, because he could be quite pretentious in his writing, --

-- and a little pompous. And I just take all that out. And then when he got talking about Bix or about Fletcher Henderson or Duke or whatever, that was good, that was great. And I had to get rid of all of the writer stuff.
Well, not many people do. In fact, --
I loved his writing, and I thought, my, where does he get that talent? Because so few guys were bright.
Well, he had talent. It was just that -- I don't know, a lot of people have the idea that if you're going to be a writer, you must be profound.
And so he'd go through that. And every one I'd take out, the next one would come in, it'd be the same thing.
Well, he wrote very-- there's a few people
that -- one of the greatest things I've read by a musician was the one that Louis Armstrong did, not about Louis, but Louis Armstrong talking, and it came out, finally, in a very small booklet.
Yeah. There was supposed to be a series of them, and only this one came out.

It may have been something that he did for Life magazine, it might have been an interview or some thing. But it's a very small booklet. And where he talks about the early funerals, where the body was in the back room of somebody's place and he said, they didn't know too much about burials there, about preparing the body. And sometimes that body would jump a little. And he says, we'd clear out of there the whole place would run out the door.
I've found that musicians were better writers than the so-called jazz writers. And I don't mean that they wrote with more feeling or warmth. They just wrote better.
